# Summary

Here we attempt to build a classification model that predicts whether an Ontario bridge needs rehabilitation soon, defined as having a Bridge Condition Index (BCI) below 70, the threshold of “good” condition, below which maintenance is usually scheduled within five years. We compared a baseline model, logistic regression and a radial basis function support vector classifier (RBF SVC) using cross-validation. On unseen test data, our final classifier, weighted RBF SVC, correctly identified 80 of the 98 bridges needing rehabilitation (recall of 0.82). However, only 38% of the bridges it flagged actually needed rehabilitation, giving an F1 score of 0.52. This means the model catches most bridges at risk but produces many false alarms, which would cost inspection time and money. Given these results, the model could help prioritize bridges for inspection, but should not replace inspections. Further work with more recent data and additional factors, such as traffic and climate, is needed before it could be used in practice.


# Introduction
Across Ontario's provincial highway network, thousands of bridges must be kept in a state of good repair to ensure safe travel and freight mobility, with annual provincial funding for transportation structures rising from $93 million in 2007/08 to $754 million in 2021/22 (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario 2021). To monitor structural depreciation, provincial bridges undergo mandatory visual inspections every two years, resulting in a Bridge Condition Index (BCI) score from 0 to 100 (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario 2021). Bridges with a BCI of 70 or above are generally considered to be in good condition, whereas scores below 70 fall into fair or poor condition where capital maintenance or rehabilitation is typically scheduled within five years (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario 2021; Ontario Ministry of Transportation 2021).

Here we ask if we can use a machine learning algorithm to predict whether an Ontario provincial bridge requires near-term rehabilitation (defined as having a current BCI below 70) versus being in good condition (a current BCI of 70 or above), given its structural, geographic, and historical characteristics. Answering this question is important because traditional visual inspections rely on qualitative assessments of material defects that can be subjective, time-consuming, and constrained by physical access—such as bridge elements located underwater, underground, or high above ground (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario 2021). Furthermore, audit reviews have found that inspection quality can vary across inspectors, with recording omissions or unverified time spent on site affecting condition records (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario 2021). If a machine learning classifier can reliably flag bridges likely to have a BCI below 70 using structural records, transportation planners could better prioritize on-site engineering inspections and allocate limited budgets before bridge health worsens.

To answer this question, we use the Bridge Conditions dataset from the Government of Ontario's Data Catalogue (Ontario Ministry of Transportation 2021). While the full dataset includes 5,053 provincial structures (2,993 bridges and 2,060 culverts), we have chosen to focus solely on the 2,993 bridges, of which 2,962 have a recorded BCI. Each row in our modeling dataset represents an individual provincial bridge with a recorded current BCI score. As predictors, we use span details, material, structure type, year built, years since last major and minor rehabilitation, length, width, owner, and region. Our binary target variable is derived from each bridge's current BCI: bridges with a current BCI below 70 are labeled as needing rehabilitation (1), while bridges with a current BCI of 70 or above are labeled as being in good condition (0).

The dataset used for this project comes from the Government of Ontario. It was sourced from the Data Catologue and can be found [here](https://data.ontario.ca/dataset/bridge-conditions).

```{python}
# Filter for Bridges only

# Rename to use snake case for consistency
rename_map = {
    "ID (SITE Ndeg)": "site_id",
    "STRUCTURE NAME": "structure_name",
    "FRENCH NAME": "french_name",
    "HIGHWAY NAME": "highway_name",
    "LATITUDE": "latitude",
    "LONGITUDE": "longitude",
    "CATEGORY": "category",
    "SUBCATEGORY 1": "subcategory",
    "TYPE 1": "structure_type",
    "MATERIAL 1": "material",
    "YEAR BUILT": "year_built",
    "LAST MAJOR REHAB": "last_major_rehab",
    "LAST MINOR REHAB": "last_minor_rehab",
    "NUMBER OF SPAN / CELLS": "num_spans_cells",
    "SPAN DETAILS (m)": "span_details_m",
    "DECK / CULVERTS LENGTH (m)": "length_m",
    "WIDTH TOTAL (m)": "width_m",
    "REGION": "region",
    "COUNTY": "county",
    "OPERATION STATUS": "operation_status",
    "OWNER": "owner",
    "LAST INSPECTION DATE": "last_inspection_date",
    "CURRENT BCI": "current_bci",
}

processed_df = processed_df.rename(columns=rename_map)

# Drop rows that don't have a CURRENT_BCI (target), 52 rows
processed_df = processed_df.dropna(subset=['current_bci'])

# Create target variable
processed_df['rehab_soon'] = (processed_df['current_bci'] < 70).astype(int)

# Parse span_details_m into total, count, max, mean, and std
def extract_span_summary(val):
    """Helper function to parse span details into total,
    count, max, mean, and std span
    """
    txt = str(val).strip()
    t_match = re.search(r"Total\s*=\s*([+-]?\d+(?:\.\d+)?)", txt, re.IGNORECASE)
    spans = [
        float(m.group(2))
        for m in re.finditer(r"\(\s*(\d+)\s*\)\s*=\s*([+-]?\d+(?:\.\d+)?)", txt)
    ]

    if spans:
        arr = np.array(spans, dtype=float)
        total_val = (
            float(t_match.group(1))
            if t_match and float(t_match.group(1)) > 0
            else float(arr.sum())
        )
        return pd.Series(
            [total_val, float(len(arr)), float(arr.max()), float(arr.mean()), float(arr.std(ddof=0))]
        )

    try:
        num = float(txt.rstrip("mM "))
        return pd.Series([num, 1.0, num, num, 0.0])
    except ValueError:
        total_val = float(t_match.group(1)) if t_match else np.nan
        return pd.Series([total_val, 0.0, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan])


processed_df[['span_total_m', 'span_count', 'span_max_m', 'span_mean_m', 'span_std_m']] = (
    processed_df['span_details_m'].apply(extract_span_summary)
)

# Group together materials
low_count_materials = [
    'Unknown',
    'Engineered Wood (Psl, etc.)',
    'Mass Concrete',
    'Plastic/Geogrid/Geocell',
    'Glue Laminated Wood',
    'Masonry/Block/Rock'
]
processed_df['material'] = processed_df['material'].replace(low_count_materials, 'Other')

# Feature Engineering
processed_df['age'] = 2020 - processed_df['year_built']

processed_df['years_since_last_rehab_major'] = 2020 - processed_df['last_major_rehab'].fillna(processed_df['year_built'])
processed_df['years_since_last_rehab_minor'] = 2020 - processed_df['last_minor_rehab'].fillna(processed_df['year_built'])


# Columns to drop
drop_columns = [
    'category',
    '_id',
    'site_id',
    'structure_name',
    'french_name',
    'highway_name',
    'latitude',
    'longitude',
    '2020', '2019', '2018', '2017', '2016', '2015', '2014', '2013', '2012',
    '2011', '2010', '2009', '2008', '2007', '2006', '2005', '2004', '2003',
    '2002', '2001', '2000',
    'year_built',
    'last_major_rehab',
    'last_minor_rehab',
    'num_spans_cells',
    'span_details_m',
    'last_inspection_date'
]
processed_df = processed_df.drop(columns=drop_columns)
# Save the processed dataframe
processed_df.to_csv('../data/processed/bridge_data_processed.csv', index=False)
```

## Model Evaluation











```{python}
# current_bci is dropped because the target was created from it (leakage).
X_train = train_df.drop(columns=["rehab_soon", "current_bci"])
y_train = train_df["rehab_soon"]

X_test = test_df.drop(columns=["rehab_soon", "current_bci"])
y_test = test_df["rehab_soon"]
```
```{python}
# Feature groups
numeric_features = [
    "age",
    "years_since_last_rehab_major",
    "years_since_last_rehab_minor",
    "length_m",
    "width_m",
    "span_total_m",
    "span_count",
    "span_max_m",
    "span_mean_m",
    "span_std_m",
]

categorical_features = [
    "material",
    "structure_type",
    "subcategory",
    "region",
    "owner",
    "operation_status",
]

drop_features = [
    "county",  # many small groups, a lot of null values
]
```
```{python}
num_pipe = make_pipeline(
    SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
    StandardScaler()
)

cat_pipe = make_pipeline(
    SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent"),
    OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False)
)

bridge_preprocessor = make_column_transformer(
    (num_pipe, numeric_features),
    (cat_pipe, categorical_features),
    ("drop", drop_features),
     verbose_feature_names_out=False
)
```

# Results

```{python}
models = {
    "Baseline (most frequent)": (
        DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
        {},
    ),
    "Logistic Regression": (
        LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
        {
            "logisticregression__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100],
            "logisticregression__class_weight": [None, "balanced"],
        },
    ),
    "RBF SVC": (
        SVC(),
        {
            "svc__C": [0.1, 1, 10, 100],
            "svc__gamma": [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1],
            "svc__class_weight": [None, "balanced"],
        },
    ),
}

grid_searches = {}
rows = []

for name, (model, grid) in models.items():
    search = GridSearchCV(
        make_pipeline(bridge_preprocessor, model),
        grid,
        cv=5,
        scoring="f1",
        return_train_score=True,
        n_jobs=-1,
    )
    search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    grid_searches[name] = search

    best = search.best_index_
    rows.append({
        "Model": name,
        "Mean train F1": search.cv_results_["mean_train_score"][best],
        "Mean validation F1": search.cv_results_["mean_test_score"][best],
        "Best settings": search.best_params_,
    })

comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Model")
comparison
```

```{python}
# RBF SVM had highest f1 score
best_model = grid_searches['RBF SVC']

y_pred = best_model.predict(X_test)

test_scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "F1": [f1_score(y_pred=y_pred, y_true=y_test)],
    "Recall": [recall_score(y_pred=y_pred, y_true=y_test)],
    "Precision": [precision_score(y_pred=y_pred, y_true=y_test)],
    "Accuracy": [accuracy_score(y_pred=y_pred, y_true=y_test)]
},)

test_scores
```

```{python}
confusion.index = ["Actually needs rehab: No", "Actually needs rehab: Yes"]
confusion.columns = ["Predicted: No", "Predicted: Yes"]
confusion
```

# Discussion

# References

## Results

### Exploratory Data Analysis

The training dataset contains 2,073 Ontario bridges, of which 229 (11%) were classified as needing rehabilitation soon (BCI < 70). The remaining 1,844 bridges (89%) did not meet this threshold (Table 1).

Bridge age appears to be associated with rehabilitation needs. Bridges requiring rehabilitation were older on average (56.2 years) than those not requiring rehabilitation (35.9 years), as shown in Table 2 and Figure 1. They also had a longer average time since major rehabilitation (31.3 versus 15.5 years).

Rehabilitation rates varied across bridge materials (Table 3 and Figure 2). Among the five most common materials, reinforced cast-in-place concrete had a rehabilitation rate of 21%, followed by steel at 18%. Weathering steel had the lowest rate at 3%.

Bridge length also differed between groups. Bridges requiring rehabilitation had a shorter average length (46.7 m) than those not requiring rehabilitation (72.6 m), as shown in Table 2. Figure 3 further illustrates the distributions of bridge lengths by rehabilitation status.

Regional differences were also observed (Table 5). The Northwestern and Eastern regions had the highest proportions requiring rehabilitation (20% and 19%, respectively), compared with 6% in the Central region.

Finally, Figure 4 shows that BCI values were concentrated primarily above the rehabilitation threshold of 70, consistent with the class imbalance observed in Table 1.

### Model Performance

Three classification models were evaluated using five-fold cross-validation: a most-frequent baseline, logistic regression, and an RBF support vector classifier (SVC). The RBF SVC achieved the highest mean validation F1 score (0.506), compared with 0.466 for logistic regression and 0.000 for the baseline.

The selected RBF SVC achieved an F1 score of 0.521, recall of 0.816, precision of 0.383, and accuracy of 0.835 on the held-out test set.

The confusion matrix showed that the model correctly identified 80 bridges requiring rehabilitation and 662 bridges not requiring rehabilitation. However, it missed 18 bridges requiring rehabilitation and incorrectly flagged 129 bridges that did not require rehabilitation.

These results suggest that the model identifies most bridges requiring rehabilitation, although its relatively low precision indicates a substantial number of false-positive predictions.
